facts.text: That squashed opening title look is deliberate: a tribute to martial arts films whose widescreen titles got compressed for VHS. Many projectionists wrongly swapped lenses mid-sequence.
Jeffrey Falcon and director Lance Mungia dreamed up the hero when Falcon tried on Mungia's thick glasses at a restaurant and looked just like Buddy Holly.
The ruins of an 1890s bank seen right about now are in Nevada. They also showed up in Michael Bay's The Island (2005).
Jeffrey Falcon did all his own stunts, with no wires and no special effects. He'd been a Hong Kong action regular in the 80s and early 90s.
The film was shot only on weekends because young Justin McGuire, who plays the Kid, still had to go to school.
The gravelly radio DJ The Werewolf is a spoof of 1950s legend Wolfman Jack.
Mungia and Falcon first planned to make the whole movie for about $25,000. It ended up costing $2 million.
The Red Elvises' songs were written before the script, so the filmmakers wrote much of the story around the music instead of the other way round.
Falcon reportedly wore the Buddy costume for eight months without washing it. That's method acting, or a biohazard.
Death is a parody of Guns N' Roses guitarist Slash. The mariachi Buddy meets is a nod to Ritchie Valens, who died in the same 1959 plane crash as Buddy Holly.
Shooting in Death Valley at around 116 degrees, the crew reportedly lost four assistant camera operators to heat stroke.
Much of the film was shot on expired Fuji film stock that was about to be thrown out, and the camera was borrowed from Panavision Hollywood.
The film was originally titled The Blade. A Hollywood Stock Exchange contest drew 4,000 name submissions, and the winner was Six-String Samurai.
The filmmakers shot a trailer first as insurance. After spending around $50,000 and shooting under 20% of the film, they cut it at Sundance to raise money to finish.
The band with the nice shoes is Igor & The Red Elvises. The big triangular instrument is an electric balalaika.
Falcon doubled as star, fight choreographer, production designer and costume designer. Mungia planned shots while Falcon built props and choreographed at 3 a.m.
The film plays loose with The Wizard of Oz: a little person says to follow the yellow brick road, and distant Lost Vegas looks like the Emerald City.
In the credits, Red Elvises member Zhenya Kolykhanov is miscredited as Zhenga Kolykhanov.
It won Slamdance awards for best editing and best cinematography in 1998, and Film Threat gave it a perfect five stars.
Chris Blackwell, the Island Records founder, saw the film at Fotokem and made an immediate bid. It became the debut release of his Palm Pictures.
Mungia drove to theaters to check the sound himself, saying sound is about 80 percent of the film. He also snuck flyers onto car windshields in parking lots.
The tiger claw Soviet soldier is Jeffrey Falcon's real-life brother, Noel Falcon.
A late-night Russian Army fight was reportedly totally ad-libbed and wrapped in two takes. That's Hong Kong style: little rehearsal.
Director Lance Mungia plays one of the archers. His next feature, The Crow: Wicked Prayer, didn't come until 2005.
It cost $2 million and earned just $124,494 in its limited theatrical run. It still became a cult favorite.
Rob Liefeld's Awesome Entertainment released a one-shot Six String Samurai comic in September 1998, written by Liefeld and Matt Hawkins.
The film was meant to be the first of a trilogy. The sequels never happened.
Fallout: New Vegas has a melee-damage achievement called New Vegas Samurai. Its art is based on this film's poster.
The film's first HD release came in 2021 from Vinegar Syndrome. It was newly scanned in 4K from the original 35mm negative, with new commentaries from Mungia and the cinematographer.
Variety's Leonard Klady called it a rock 'n' roll Mad Max served up Cantonese style.
